before: std::unique_ptr<T> from <memory> owns one object and destroys it automatically. std::make_unique<int>(7) constructs a heap-allocated int and returns its owner. Prefer this to raw owning new/delete.
unique_ptr cannot be copied. Moving it transfers ownership and specifically leaves the source pointer empty. Test a pointer before dereferencing it; *q accesses its owned int.
In a condition a nonempty smart pointer is true. The comparison p == nullptr checks whether p is empty; this check does not access a missing object.

Expected output or behavior: true
7
. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Change the owned value after transferring it, using only q and checking q first. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: std::unique_ptr owns an object and destroys it when ownership ends. std::make_unique<int>(7), from <memory>, creates an integer in separately managed storage and returns its owner. You do not need to write new and delete yourself.
A unique_ptr cannot be copied. Moving it transfers ownership to the destination. Unlike a general moved-from value, a moved-from unique_ptr is specifically guaranteed to be empty.
if (q) checks whether q has a target. *q then reaches the owned integer. Comparing p with nullptr only checks whether p is empty; it does not try to read a target.
The program prints true, then 7 on the next line. p is empty after the move. q owns the integer and can read it after the check.
Only q owns the integer after this transfer. When q is destroyed, it also destroys the owned integer. An observing raw pointer would not take on that cleanup responsibility.

before.question: Replace std::move(p) with p when initializing q. What happens?
choices: Both owners safely share the int
Compilation fails because unique_ptr is noncopyable
p is copied and becomes empty
before.explanation: Copy construction is deleted. Shared ownership requires a different, deliberate type, not a copied unique_ptr.

after.question: Replace std::move(p) with p when creating q. What happens?
choices: Both pointers share ownership of the integer.
The compiler rejects the attempt to copy a unique_ptr.
p is copied and automatically becomes empty.
after.explanation: unique_ptr forbids copying. Ownership can be transferred with a move, but it cannot be duplicated this way.
